title: Atomic structure
learningObjective: Know what is meant by the terms atom and molecule; Know the structure of an atom in terms of the positions, relative masses and relative charges of sub-atomic particles; Know what is meant by the terms atomic number, mass number, isotopes and relative atomic mass (Aᵣ); Be able to calculate the relative atomic mass of an element (Aᵣ) from isotopic abundances

sections.title: Atomic structure — the chapter map
sections.markdown:
Take a piece of copper and imagine cutting it in half, then in half again,
on and on. The thought experiment ends at a definite stopping point:
eventually you reach the smallest piece of copper that can exist — and at
that stage you are holding a single copper **[[atom]]**. You *could* split
that atom further, into protons, neutrons and electrons, but the moment you
do, you no longer have copper: the pieces are not copper, they are
sub-atomic particles. That is the definition of the atom — *the
smallest piece of an element that can still be recognised as that element*.

The 118 elements are the building blocks from which everything is made,
from a simple substance such as carbon to something as complex as DNA, and
every one of those elements is built from atoms. What makes one element
different from another is what this chapter is about: the numbers of
protons, neutrons and electrons inside the atom. And the story reaches
further than Earth: new atoms are produced in stars, which is why the story
of the atom is also, quietly, the story of the universe.

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

- say what **atom** and **molecule** mean, in mark-scheme language;
- describe the structure of the atom — where the protons, neutrons and
  electrons are, and their **relative masses and charges**;
- define **atomic number**, **mass number**, **isotopes** and **relative
  atomic mass (Aᵣ)**;
- calculate a **relative atomic mass** from isotopic abundances, exactly as
  the worked example does for boron (§s08).

:::key-point
An atom is the smallest piece of an element that can still be recognised as
that element. Split it into protons, neutrons and electrons and you no
longer have the element — that splitting happens only in nuclear processes
(nuclear bombs, nuclear reactors, radioactive decay), never in chemistry.
:::

:::prior-knowledge
From Lesson u1:c02 (Elements, compounds and mixtures) you know that an
element contains only one type of atom and that all 118 elements are listed
in the Periodic Table — this chapter finally defines what "type of atom"
means. From Lesson u1:c01 you know particles in solids, liquids and gases;
the electron behaviour you will meet here (§s03) is the same "constantly
moving" picture. Nothing from KS3 beyond "everything is made of atoms" is
assumed — if that phrase was hazy, it stops being hazy today.
:::

:::misconception
"If you keep cutting copper small enough, the tiny pieces are still copper."
No — below the level of the **atom** there is no copper any more: protons,
neutrons and electrons are not copper. The atom is the floor for *chemical*
identity; only nuclear processes (not chemical ones) go below it.
:::

:::exam-hint
"State what is meant by *atom*" is a 1-mark definition: *"the smallest
piece of an element that can still be recognised as that element"* or the
equivalent mark-scheme line *"smallest particle of an element"*. Do not
answer with the structure (protons/neutrons/electrons) — that is a
different question (spec 1.15) and earns nothing here.
:::

:::quick-check

Question-bank join: spec 1.14 × 2 items — the smallest piece that is still
the element; whether atoms can be split by chemical means.
:::

sections.title: Atoms and molecules
sections.markdown:
Atoms rarely stay single. They can be joined together to make
**[[molecule]]**s: a molecule consists of **two or more atoms chemically
bonded (by [[covalent-bond]]s)**. One point repays care, and examiners love
it: the atoms in a molecule can be **the same element or
different elements**. A hydrogen molecule, H₂, is two
hydrogen atoms bonded together — one element only, and still a molecule. A
water molecule, H₂O, is two hydrogen atoms and an oxygen atom bonded
together. In diagrams like these the lines between atoms represent the
chemical bonds.

Splitting an atom into smaller pieces is not a chemical process at all. As
§s01 established, that only happens in **nuclear processes** — nuclear
bombs, nuclear reactors, radioactive decay. Chemistry, the whole subject
you are studying, happens *above* that floor: it rearranges how atoms are
joined, it never splits them.

One caution before we go inside the atom. You may have seen diagrams in
which [[electron]]s are drawn orbiting the nucleus rather like planets around
the sun. That picture is **misleading**. Electrons are constantly
moving, and it is impossible to know exactly where an electron is at any
moment; what you can say is that it has a particular **energy** and is
likely to be found in a certain **region of space** at some particular
distance from the nucleus. Electrons with different energies are found at
different distances from the nucleus — that energy-region picture is the
one to carry through the course.

:::

:::cross-curricular
**Physics:** everything in §s02's nuclear list — nuclear bombs, nuclear
reactors, radioactive decay — is physics territory: chemistry cannot split
the atom, and the energy side of that line belongs to your physics lessons.
**Stars:** new atoms are produced in stars — stellar nuclear fusion is
where the elements' story begins.
:::key-point
A molecule is two or more atoms chemically bonded (covalently). The atoms
may be the same element (H₂) or different elements (H₂O). And the
planet-orbit picture of electrons is misleading: electrons have particular
energies and are likely to be found in certain regions of space, not on
fixed tracks.
:::

:::misconception
"A molecule must contain at least two different elements." No — H₂ is a
molecule of one element only. What makes it a molecule is **two or more
atoms chemically bonded**, not the variety of elements. (One atom alone is
an atom; two bonded atoms are a molecule, same element or not.)
:::

:::exam-hint
Write molecular formulae with subscripts: H₂ and H₂O, never "H2" / "H2O" —
in "explain/draw a molecule" answers the subscript carries the meaning
(two hydrogens in H₂O). If asked to draw the molecules, use the standard
convention: lines between atoms represent the bonds.
:::

:::quick-check

Question-bank join: spec 1.14 × 3 items — define molecule; is H₂ a molecule
of a compound or of an element; why the planet-orbit diagram is only a
model.
:::

sections.title: Inside the atom — protons, neutrons and electrons
sections.markdown:
Atoms are made of **[[proton]]s**, **[[neutron]]s** and **[[electron]]s** — particles
smaller than an atom — hence the name **sub-atomic
particles**. The protons and neutrons sit together in the **[[nucleus]]**
at the centre of the atom; the electrons occupy the space around it.

How small is the nucleus really? Scale a helium
atom up to the size of a sports hall and the nucleus would be no more than
the size of a **grain of sand**. Almost all of the atom is empty space —
yet almost all of its **mass** is in that grain of sand, because electrons
have a far smaller mass than protons and neutrons.

The numbers you must know are **relative** values — measured against each
other, because the real values are incredibly small (it would take about
600 000 000 000 000 000 000 000, that is 6 × 10²³, protons to weigh 1 g).
One small table carries the whole story:

| Particle | Relative mass | Relative charge |
|----------|---------------|-----------------|
| proton   | 1             | +1              |
| neutron  | 1             | 0               |
| electron | 1/1836        | −1              |

Protons and neutrons have (relative) mass 1 — the electron's mass,
1/1836, is so small it is usually treated as negligible when counting an
atom's mass. Charges: the proton is +1, the neutron is 0 (neutral), the
electron is −1.

:::key-point
Relative masses and charges: proton mass 1, charge +1;
neutron mass 1, charge 0; electron mass 1/1836, charge −1. Protons and
neutrons are in the nucleus; electrons are outside it. Virtually all the
atom's mass is in the nucleus.
:::

:::misconception
"The electron's mass of 1/1836 means a negative mass." No — 1/1836 is the
**relative mass** (about 0.0005 of a proton's); the **−1 is its charge**,
a separate column. Mass tiny, charge negative: keep the two properties
apart and the table reads cleanly.
:::

:::exam-hint
"State the relative masses and relative charges of the proton, neutron and
electron" is a stock 3-mark question (spec 1.15 verbatim). Learn the table
as a 2 × 3 grid and write the charge **with its sign**: +1, 0, −1. A
missing − sign loses the mark even when the number is right.
:::

:::quick-check

Question-bank join: spec 1.15 × 3 items — where each particle sits; the
relative masses; the relative charges (signs included).
:::

sections.title: Atomic number and mass number
sections.markdown:
Two numbers label every atom. The **number of protons** in an atom's
nucleus is its **[[atomic-number]]** (sometimes called the **proton
number**):

> atomic number = number of protons

Each of the 118 elements has its own atomic number — no two elements share
it. If an atom has 8 protons, it must be an oxygen atom; the atomic number
doesn't just describe the element, it **defines** it. A playful way to see
it: we could talk about "a wristwatch made from the element with atomic
number 79" instead of "a gold wristwatch" — true, but nobody talks that
way, because names are easier.

The second number counts the whole nucleus. The **[[mass-number]]**
(sometimes known as the **nucleon number**) is the total number of protons
and neutrons:

> mass number = number of protons + number of neutrons

For any particular atom the two numbers can be written as a label on the
symbol — for example cobalt, written in nuclide-style notation as
⁵⁹₂₇Co. This particular cobalt atom contains 27 protons (the atomic
number, bottom-left); to bring the total of protons and neutrons up to 59
(the mass number, top-left) it must also contain 32 neutrons. Rearranged,
that is the counting formula you will use constantly:

> number of neutrons = mass number − atomic number

One more caution, and it matters for the Periodic Table
(§s10): the number above each symbol in the International GCSE Periodic
Table papers is a **relative atomic mass, not a mass number**. In most
cases it happens to equal the mass number of the most common isotope — the
the only exceptions are **chlorine (35.5)** and **copper
(63.5)**, and §s06 explains exactly why those two break the pattern.

:::key-point
atomic number = number of protons (defines the element). mass number =
protons + neutrons. neutrons = mass number − atomic number. In nuclide
notation (⁵⁹₂₇Co) the top-left number is the mass number, the bottom-left
the atomic number.
:::

:::misconception
"The bigger number printed on the Periodic Table is the mass number." Not
always — on exam-paper Periodic Tables that number is the **relative
atomic mass**. It matches the most common isotope's mass number for most
elements, but chlorine (35.5) and copper (63.5) prove it is not a mass
number: no atom contains half a neutron.
:::

:::exam-hint
Symbols with two letters: **first capital, second lower-case**. The classic
trap is CO versus Co — "CO" is carbon monoxide (a compound), "Co"
is cobalt (an element). Case is not decoration in chemistry; it is the
difference between an element and a compound.
:::

:::quick-check

Question-bank join: spec 1.16 × 3 items — define atomic number; define mass
number; neutrons from mass number − atomic number (cobalt 59/27). spec 1.15
× 1 item — which particles the two numbers count.
:::

sections.title: Isotopes — same element, different mass
sections.markdown:
The number of neutrons in an atom can vary slightly. Carbon is the classic
example: there are three kinds of carbon atom, called **carbon-12**,
**carbon-13** and **carbon-14**.
All of them have 6 protons — every carbon atom does, because 6 is carbon's
atomic number — but their neutron counts differ, so their mass numbers
differ too. These different atoms of the same element are called
**[[isotope]]s**:

> Isotopes are atoms (of the same element) which have the same atomic
> number but different mass numbers — the same number of protons but
> different numbers of neutrons.

Does the isotope change how the element behaves? No — and the reason is
worth memorising because it is the bridge to the rest of chemistry. The
fact that isotopes have varying numbers of neutrons makes **no difference
to their chemical reactions**: chemical properties (how something reacts)
are controlled by the number **and arrangement of the electrons**, and
that is identical for all three carbon isotopes. Carbon-12 and carbon-14
are chemically the same element; where they differ is mass (and, for some
isotopes, nuclear stability — a nuclear property, not a chemical one).

:::key-point
Isotopes = same atomic number (same protons), different mass numbers
(different neutrons). Chemistry is unchanged between isotopes because
chemical reactions depend on the electrons, which are identical.
:::

:::misconception
"Isotopes are the radioactive versions of an element." No — isotope just
means *same protons, different neutrons*. Carbon-12 and carbon-13 are
stable isotopes; radioactivity is a separate nuclear property that only
*some* isotopes (like carbon-14) have. Don't fold nuclear behaviour into
a definition that is only about particle counts.
:::

:::exam-hint
"Explain what isotopes are" scores with the paired wording: *same number
of protons (same atomic number), different numbers of neutrons (different
mass numbers)*. Both halves must appear — protons alone, or neutrons
alone, is half an answer and half a mark. And "explain the difference
between two isotopes" wants the neutrons/mass number, never "one is more
reactive".
:::

:::quick-check

Question-bank join: spec 1.16 × 2 items — define isotopes; why ¹²C, ¹³C and
¹⁴C react identically.
:::

sections.title: Relative atomic mass — the 35.5 puzzle
sections.markdown:
Look up chlorine on the [[periodic-table]] and you meet a paradox. The number
beside chlorine appears to be a **mass number of 35.5**. Try the
§s04 formula on it:

> number of neutrons = 35.5 − 17 = 18.5

It is not possible to have **half a neutron** — so something must be wrong
with this. And something is: 35.5 is not a mass number at all. It is the
**[[relative-atomic-mass]] (Aᵣ)** of chlorine. Chlorine consists of two
isotopes, ³⁵Cl and ³⁷Cl, and a naturally occurring sample contains a
**mixture of these** — so the 35.5 is an average across the whole sample,
not the mass of any single atom.

A plain average would not do, because the isotopes are not present in
equal amounts. The tool for this is the same one you use in maths when
some values count for more than others: the
**[[weighted-average]]** (or **weighted mean**). The relative atomic mass
is a weighted average of the isotope masses, weighted by how much of each
isotope is present in a naturally occurring sample. That single sentence
is the definition behind spec 1.16's last term — and §s07 and §s08 turn it
into a calculation you can perform.

:::

:::cross-curricular
**Maths:** the weighted mean is a taught GCSE maths skill — values scaled
by weights before averaging. Aᵣ is that exact calculation applied to
isotope masses and abundances; the maths department's "weighted average"
and chemistry's "relative atomic mass" are one and the same operation.
:::key-point
35.5 for chlorine is a **relative atomic mass (Aᵣ)**, not a mass number —
no atom has half a neutron. Aᵣ is a weighted average of the isotope masses
across a naturally occurring sample; chlorine's sample is a mixture of
³⁵Cl and ³⁷Cl.
:::

:::misconception
"Chlorine's mass number is 35.5, so a chlorine atom has 18.5 neutrons."
Twice wrong — no chlorine atom has 18.5 neutrons (impossible), and 35.5 is
not any atom's mass number. Real chlorine atoms are ³⁵Cl (18 neutrons) or
³⁷Cl (20 neutrons); the 35.5 is the sample's weighted average.
:::

:::exam-hint
If an exam gives a non-integer "mass number" (35.5, 63.5), it is telling
you the quantity is a **relative atomic mass** — say so explicitly.
Naming the quantity correctly ("Aᵣ, not mass number") is usually a mark
in itself on questions of this type.
:::

:::quick-check

Question-bank join: spec 1.16 × 3 items — why 35.5 cannot be a mass number;
what Aᵣ is an average *of*; why a plain average would not do.
:::

sections.title: Counting the number of electrons in an atom
sections.markdown:
Here is the question you can now almost answer for yourself: given an
element, how do you count the electrons in its atom? The full
charge-balance argument arrives in §s09 — the anchor that everything else
hangs from comes *here*: **the number of protons is the same as the atomic
number of the element**. Count protons by looking up the atomic number; electrons
then follow (§s09); neutrons come from mass number − atomic number
(§s04). One look-up, three particle counts.

The hint box also closes the chlorine story from §s06, and it is worth
reading slowly because it is examiner-true reasoning. **Relative atomic
mass** is defined as the *average mass of an atom, taking into account the
amount of each isotope present in a naturally occurring sample of an
element* (Chapter 5 builds on this further). Apply that to
chlorine: the Aᵣ of 35.5 is **closer to 35 than to 37**, so a naturally
occurring sample of chlorine must contain **more ³⁵Cl than ³⁷Cl** — the
average sits nearer the isotope that contributes more.

That "amount of each isotope" is the **[[isotopic-abundance]]** — the
percentage of each isotope in the sample. Knowing the abundances, you can
stop *reasoning about* the average and *calculate* it, in exactly the way
you would calculate a weighted average in maths — which is exactly what
the next section's worked example does.

:::key-point
Protons = atomic number (one Periodic-Table look-up powers all three
particle counts). Aᵣ = the average mass of an atom taking the isotopic
abundances into account; the average lies closest to the most abundant
isotope.
:::

:::misconception
"Chlorine's Aᵣ of 35.5 means the sample is mostly ³⁷Cl, since 37 is the
bigger isotope." No — the weighted average is **closer to 35**, which is
only possible if **³⁵Cl is the more abundant** isotope. Distance from the
average tells you which isotope dominates; bigger isotope ≠ bigger share.
:::

:::exam-hint
"Explain why a sample of chlorine contains more ³⁵Cl than ³⁷Cl" scores by
one line: *the relative atomic mass (35.5) is closer to 35 than to 37*. Quote the closeness argument — it is the whole mark.
:::

:::quick-check

Question-bank join: spec 1.17 × 2 items — define isotopic abundance; which
chlorine isotope dominates and why. spec 1.16 × 1 item — the Aᵣ definition
(average, abundances taken into account).
:::

sections.title: Worked example — the relative atomic mass of boron
sections.markdown:
This worked example turns §s07's definition into a routine. A naturally occurring sample of boron contains
**20% ¹⁰B and 80% ¹¹B**. Calculate the relative atomic mass.

The method — **imagine there are exactly 100 atoms** — makes the
percentages do the work:

- 20% of 100 atoms = 20 atoms, each of mass 10 → total mass 20 × 10
- 80% of 100 atoms = 80 atoms, each of mass 11 → total mass 80 × 11

Add the masses, divide by the number of atoms, and the average falls out:

> relative atomic mass = (20 × 10 + 80 × 11) ÷ 100 = (200 + 880) ÷ 100 =
> **10.8**

Therefore the relative atomic mass of boron is **10.8**. Notice what the
number tells you before you check it: 10.8 sits much closer to 11 than to
10, exactly as §s07 predicts for a sample that is 80% ¹¹B.

The same method works even if there are **three or four different
isotopes**: multiply each isotope's mass by its abundance, add all the
products, divide by 100 (when abundances are percentages). The
imagine-100-atoms framing survives every exam version of this question.

:::worked-example
Boron: 20% ¹⁰B, 80% ¹¹B. Imagine 100 atoms → 20 atoms of mass 10, 80 of
mass 11. Total mass = 20 × 10 + 80 × 11 = 1080. Divide by 100 atoms:
Aᵣ = **10.8**. Mark lines: (1) multiply each mass by its abundance;
(2) add the products; (3) divide by 100; (4) quote 10.8 (no units — Aᵣ is
a relative quantity).
:::

:::maths-skills
The skill is the **weighted mean**, in the exact form maths uses: multiply
each value by its weight, add, divide by the total weight. Here the values
are isotope masses (10, 11) and the weights are the abundances (20, 80).
The imagine-100 trick converts percentages into counts so you never have
to manipulate percentage fractions under exam pressure.
:::

:::misconception
"The relative atomic mass of boron should be a whole number, like a mass
number." No — Aᵣ is an average over a mixture, so it is usually not a
whole number (boron 10.8, chlorine 35.5, copper 63.5). Whole numbers
belong to individual isotopes (mass numbers 10 and 11); the element's
Aᵣ averages across them.
:::

:::exam-hint
Show the full weighted-mean line — (20 × 10 + 80 × 11) ÷ 100 — not just
the answer. The three method steps carry the marks; a bare "10.8" with no
working risks losing method marks if any slip occurs. Quote the final
value **without units**.
:::

:::quick-check

Question-bank join: spec 1.17 × 3 items — reproduce the boron calculation; a
two-isotope Aᵣ with different abundances; the three-isotope generalisation.
:::

sections.title: The electrons
sections.markdown:
One charge argument finishes the particle census. The charge on a proton
(+1) is **equal but opposite** to the charge on an electron (−1), and an
atom is neutral — so the two charges must cancel exactly:

> number of electrons = number of protons

Two checks: an oxygen atom (atomic number 8) has 8 protons, so it must
also have 8 electrons; a chlorine atom (atomic number 17) has 17
protons and therefore 17 electrons. The key feature throughout is knowing
the **atomic number** — one look-up on the Periodic Table (§s10) and all
three counts follow: protons from the atomic number, electrons from the
protons, neutrons from mass number − atomic number.

Why, then, is the atomic number *defined* in terms of protons rather than
electrons, when either count starts from the other in a neutral atom? The
answer matters for the whole course: the number of electrons can
**change in chemical reactions**, for example when atoms form
**[[ion]]**s (Chapter 7) — but the number of protons in the nucleus never
changes chemically. Protons are the stable identity; electrons are the
reactive surface. That is why "number of protons = atomic number" is the
definition of record, and "electrons = protons" is merely true for neutral
atoms.

:::key-point
Charge balance: proton +1 vs electron −1, equal and opposite, so in an
atom electrons = protons. The atomic number is defined via protons because
protons never change chemically, while electrons can (ions, Chapter 7).
:::

:::misconception
"An oxygen atom has 8 protons and 10 electrons, like its mass number
suggests." No — mass number counts **protons + neutrons**, never
electrons. A neutral oxygen atom: 8 protons, 8 electrons, and (for ¹⁶O)
8 neutrons. Electrons follow the *atomic* number, not the mass number.
:::

:::exam-hint
"Explain why the number of protons in an atom must always equal the number
of electrons" is a stock end-of-chapter part (d) — and the marks
are: *charges equal and opposite* (+1/−1) *and atoms are neutral, so the
charges must cancel*. Both halves, in that order.
:::

:::quick-check

Question-bank join: spec 1.15 × 2 items — the charge-cancellation argument;
count all three particles for oxygen. spec 1.16 × 1 item — why the atomic
number is defined via protons.
:::

sections.title: The Periodic Table — counting particles from the chart
sections.markdown:
Everything in this chapter runs on one reference chart. Atoms are arranged
in the **[[periodic-table]]** in order of **increasing atomic number** —
that ordering *is* the chapter's payoff: the chart is a particle-counting
device. (Chapter 4 deals in detail with everything else the Periodic
Table tells you; the Periodic Table in your exam paper carries
the full version.)

Most Periodic Tables show **two numbers** against each symbol, and the
warning is blunt: be careful to choose the right one. The atomic
number will **always be the smaller number**. The other number is either
the **mass number of the most common isotope** of the element or the
**relative atomic mass** of the element (§s06 showed you why those are not
the same thing — chlorine's 35.5). The Periodic Table you are using will
clarify which; exam papers always state their convention.

The complete counting recipe for any atom:

- the number of **protons** = the atomic number (the smaller number);
- the number of **electrons** = the number of protons;
- the number of **neutrons** = mass number − atomic number.

Three lines, one chart, every atom on the syllabus. §s11 works the recipe
end-to-end on uranium.

:::key-point
Periodic Table recipe: protons = atomic number (always the smaller
number); electrons = protons; neutrons = mass number − atomic number.
Watch the second number in the cell: mass number (most common isotope) or
relative atomic mass — they are not the same quantity.
:::

:::misconception
"The two numbers in a Periodic Table cell are the mass number and the
atomic number." Only sometimes — the larger number is the **relative
atomic mass** on exam papers (chlorine 35.5, copper 63.5), which equals
the most common isotope's mass number for most elements but not all. Read
the paper's convention; do not assume.
:::

:::exam-hint
When a question says "use the Periodic Table", it is licensing the
three-line recipe. Write the atomic number down first (from the chart),
then run the recipe in order: protons → electrons → neutrons. Stating the
atomic number explicitly protects the whole chain of marks.
:::

:::quick-check

Question-bank join: spec 1.16 × 3 items — which number is which in a cell;
the three-line recipe; apply it to a named element.
:::

sections.title: Worked example — uranium, and the chapter close
sections.markdown:
This worked example runs the §s10 recipe on a heavy atom. The symbol for
uranium is given in a Periodic Table as **²³⁸U (uranium, atomic number
92)**. Calculate the number of protons, neutrons and electrons in an atom
of uranium.

- The atomic number is the **smaller** number, so uranium's atomic number
  is 92 → a uranium atom contains **92 protons**.
- Protons = electrons → **92 electrons**.
- Neutrons = mass number − atomic number = 238 − 92 = **146**.

Same three lines as always — the atom just gets heavier. (For this you
will need the Periodic Table in your exam paper.)

The chapter-closing skill list is worth self-checking: particle locations
and charges; counting the particles in a fluorine atom; reading
nuclide-style symbols like ⁵⁶Fe and ⁹³₄₁Nb; chlorine's two isotopes; and a
run of relative-atomic-mass calculations — lithium, magnesium with three
isotopes, and lead with four. This lesson's practice is wired to the
question bank below.

One last fact for the road: considering only the most
common isotope of each element, there is **only one element that has more
protons than neutrons**. Work it out with the recipe — the answer is
hydrogen, whose most common atom (¹H) has 1 proton and **0** neutrons;
every other element's most common isotope carries at least as many
neutrons as protons.

:::worked-example
Uranium ²³⁸U, atomic number 92: atomic number = smaller number = 92 →
92 protons; electrons = protons → 92 electrons; neutrons = 238 − 92 =
146. Mark lines: (1) identify the atomic number as the smaller number;
(2) protons from atomic number; (3) electrons = protons; (4) subtract for
neutrons.
:::

:::key-point
The counting recipe is atom-independent: ²³⁸U → 92 protons, 92 electrons,
146 neutrons. And a chapter-closing curiosity — hydrogen-1
is the only most-common-isotope atom with more protons than neutrons
(1 proton, 0 neutrons).
:::

:::misconception
"Heavy atoms like uranium have far more electrons than protons." No —
charge balance holds for every atom: 92 protons, 92 electrons. What grows
faster in heavy atoms is the **neutron** count (146 here), which is
exactly why neutrons = mass number − atomic number is the line you keep
computing.
:::

:::exam-hint
For "state the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons" answers,
present all three counts in order (protons, electrons, neutrons) with the
substitution shown for neutrons (238 − 92 = 146). The substitution line is
the method mark; the three numbers are the answer marks.
:::

:::quick-check

Question-bank join: spec 1.16 × 2 items — reproduce the uranium counts; the
hydrogen-1 exception. spec 1.17 × 1 item — the lead four-isotope weighted
mean.
:::

:::summary
- An **[[atom]]** is the smallest piece of an element still recognisable
  as that element; a **[[molecule]]** is two or more atoms chemically
  bonded (H₂, H₂O). Only nuclear processes split atoms — chemistry never
  does.
- Atoms contain **protons** (mass 1, charge +1) and **neutrons** (mass 1,
  charge 0) in the nucleus, with **electrons** (mass 1/1836, charge −1)
  outside; virtually all the mass is nuclear.
- **Atomic number** = protons (defines the element); **mass number** =
  protons + neutrons; **neutrons** = mass number − atomic number;
  electrons = protons (neutral atoms).
- **Isotopes**: same atomic number, different mass numbers — chemically
  identical, because chemistry belongs to the electrons.
- **Aᵣ** is the weighted average of isotope masses across a natural
  sample (chlorine 35.5: mostly ³⁵Cl; boron 10.8 from 20%/80%).
- Periodic Table: ordered by increasing atomic number; smaller number =
  atomic number; run the three-line recipe for any atom.
:::
